utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. As you know, our hearing will continue until a quarter to 2.00. I would like to say good morning to the witness, to the lawyers, the Prosecutor, and all of the personnel of the courtroom. I would like to give the floor now to Madam Nozica to continue her questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Marijan.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Before we continue the interrogation, let me go back to something that remained unclear yesterday. When you were answering Judge Antonetti's question about doctrine, you said that the HVO didn't have many trained former officers from the JNA; is that right? Because the transcript reads that there were many. Could you please explain in one sentence only to make things clear.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the HVO had very few trained officers from the Yugoslav People's Army. It was a very small share of the overall number of officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marijan, yesterday in our examination we arrived at the interpretation of the provisions of Article 10 of the decree on the armed forces of the 3rd of July of 1992 and October 1992 respectively. I would now like to proceed to item 11 of your report to explain the structure of the Department of Defence to see what sectors there were, who was working there, et cetera, and then we'll return to Article 10 to clarify which of these duties the Department of Defence actually implemented, whether it had enough personnel to do what it -- what it had to do, et cetera. That will assist us in interpreting the provisions of Article 10. In your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, Ms. Nozica. I feel that I have to take up a point which last night there was no time to take up, and it was the last answer of the witness before Judge Antonetti then intervened. You had asked about Article 10, paragraph 3 mainly, and you had before told the witness, very correctly, that as he is not a lawyer, he is not really qualified to interpret the law. Nevertheless, his next answer was that the formulation of a plan for the deployment of the armed forces was not the task of the Ministry of the Defence. I think, Mr. Marijan, what you can say is that you have no trace of any such activity carried out by the Ministry of Defence, but you cannot say that it was not a duty when that is what the decree very clearly says. What is your reaction to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is a fact that Article 10 of the decree says as much, but the plan for the employment of the armed forces was not actually a task of the head of the Department of Defence. This -- this brings us back to a problem. The task of the Department of Defence will become more clear once we explain its structure then you will understand why -- you will understand my statement, because this way we limit ourselves to this statement that you mentioned, and I'm afraid that we will arrive at no conclusion whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, I do not think that unable to understand what you're saying even up to now, but I leave it at that for the moment. You simply are saying that the law was something different than the law was. The law says that one of the task of this and you say it was not. Thank you, Ms. Nozica. Excuse me interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, it is exactly for the reason that I think that some things will become clear if we dwell on Article 10 as regards the structure of the Department of Defence. That's why the -- these questions, what were the tasks of the Department of Defence and what it was able to do can -- can become clearer by examining the witness. Then we will see what they were able to do and what they were charged to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have full confidence in that you will be able to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, in item 11 you state when Mr. Stojic was appointed. Could you please very briefly say -- state his profession and explain the situation with Mr. Stojic, how that fits into the former system, whether it's a deviation from that former system, and the overall situation about the appointment of Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Stojic became head of the Department of Defence on the 3rd of July, 1992. That's when he was appointed. Mr. Stojic by training is an economist, a civilian, that is, a person without military training apart, probably, from his -- his conscript service in the Yugoslav People's Army. He had a civilian position, and that is a great difference between the head of the Department of Defence and what was in place in Yugoslavia. In Yugoslavia, defence fell within the remit of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, what we would nowadays call Ministry of Defence. The federal secretary was a soldier, and he was inside the military hierarchy within the command and control structure. In peacetime, he was in control of the entire armed forces. And speaking about Mr. Kadijevic, we can say that later on it became evident that even in wartime he pulled all the strings. In the late 1980s in Yugoslavia when there were demands for democratisation, one of the demands was a civilian become Federal Secretary of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, what had Mr. Stojic been doing before he was appointed head of the Department of Defence?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a logistics assistant of the commander of the HVO, and when he joined the Department of Defence he actually widened the scope of his tasks and responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is another important piece of information. How long did he stay in that position?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, he was in that position until the 15th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, I will say that evidence about the appointment of Mr. Stojic is -- are P 297, and the document corroborating his -- his taking over the position is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The number escaped us. Interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, I will have to speed up, because yesterday I took too long. When you say that the head of the Department of Defence was a civilian, he also had a deputy. Item 12 clearly shows when he was appointed. Can you tell us whether the deputy head was also a civilian, and what were his responsibilities in the Department of Defence?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic's deputy was a civilian. He was appointed on the 15th of January, 1993. He had been in that position earlier, and he was in charge of the so-called civilian sector of the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Once we reach the provisions regulating the internal structure, we will see what the civilian sector comprised. To who did the head of the Department of Defence report? Who was he answerable to, and what was the character of the reports he submitted?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the Department of Defence reported to the HVO. That's where he sent his reports. They were semi-annual and annual reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did he attend meetings, and did he speak about the problems of the Department of Defence, and not only problems but also everything that was within the remit of the HVO. Did he make motions for acts and legislation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was indeed discussion about defence-related issues at HVO meetings. In item 13 I mention the precise -- the information's more precise. In January 1992, on nine occasions there was discussion about defence, and a total of 27 regular and 6 interim sessions were held in the first half of the year, and issues under the jurisdiction of the Department of Defence were presented in 26 items of the agenda. Based on these discussions, the HVO accepted reports and also gave instructions to the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether at these HVO sessions there was discussion about the security situation? Did the head of the Department of Defence give information about that, and who else did so?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a frequently discussed issue, the security situation. Mr. Stojic gave information about that on several occasions, and he was -- and, sorry, the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO was also summoned several times to give his view of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, you spoke about semi-annual and annual reports that the Department of Defence submitted and that were discussed at HVO meetings. Did they also include the report of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the November report for 1992, it says that the report of the Main Staff for reasons of secrecy is submitted separately. It was kept in the cabinet of the president of the HZ HB and the president of the HVO, but all members of the HVO had access to that report. And that was also subsequent practice. In the first half of 1993, the part relating to the Main Staff is missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, please, sir, say very briefly because we are to pass on to these acts instantly what was the organisation and structure of the Department of Defence and which provisions are relevant?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Department of Defence of the HVO consisted of sectors, administrations, offices, and the Main Staff. The underlying document that regulated the structure of the Department of Defence was signed by President Boban on the 15th of September, 1992. The name of the document is "Decision on the foundations of the organisation of the Department of Defence." Based on this, Mr. Stojic, as head, signed a document that lays out the details of this decision of Mr. Boban. This decision of Mr. Stojic was dated 17 October 1992, and Mr. Boban subsequently approved that decision. Let me also mention that in May 1993, a new decision was drawn up about the internal organisation of the Department of Defence. It differs from the first one only in that a welfare administration was added to the existing structural elements. So this is a new -- within the sector for supply, procurement and production. This is the difference to the decision dated October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us now go to document 586. This is -- it can be found in binder X. The Exhibit number is P 00586. You have it in front of you. So this is the decision that you said was passed by Mr. Boban, and let us go item by item to see how the Department of Defence was structured in September 1992. Item I reads -- I will ask you for a comment of item 1 or whatever I think is relevant. You can read for yourself.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, item I of this decision says that: "This decision shall define the basic principles of organisation of the Defence Department. The principal sectors including the Main Staff," which is part of the department. Item II says that the head of the department shall direct the work of the department. And furthermore, attached to the head are a military council and a chief inspectorate who shall perform their duties in accordance with the decree and guide-lines issued by the president of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Stop for a moment, please. Tell me, have you seen whether the military council -- or tell me first which provisions regulate the activities of the military council.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- the pertinent document is the act on the military forces of the HZ HB that govern the work of the military council and the chief inspectorate.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the period when Mr. Stojic was head of the Department of Defence, do you know of a document establishing these two bodies?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The military council was established later, I believe, in December 1993, but then Mr. Stojic was no longer head of the department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It goes on to say the head in the administrative and technical sense is aided in his work by the cabinet of the head and the Office of General and Legal Affairs -- sorry, General Affairs and the Information System as separate organisational units. What is this cabinet? What do you understand it to be, and what was the Office of General Affairs and Information -- the Information System?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cabinet of the head consisted of persons directly connected to Mr. Stojic and his work. That is secretaries, drivers, and the security. Those were staff absolutely necessary to make it possible for the head to do his work as technical support, and the Office of General Affairs can also be considered part of that. To put it briefly, it was something of the archive of the head of the department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Let us move on to item III. The head had a deputy. The deputy head is directly responsible for the civilian sector. And item V -- or, rather, item III mentions its organisational units. We don't need to read them out.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me please add that under item III(1), what is mentioned is an administration with a very long and cumbersome name. It will not be mentioned subsequently. Later on it will be called administration for defence affairs and the administration. Even in Croatian this is a cumbersome original name, and it must be so in the translation too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Talking about this administration, when did it -- when did it start functioning? You mentioned that in your report, but I'm condensing things now.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look that up.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Once we get there, I will remind you. Let us move on to item IV, which reads: For some sections the department head shall have assistants, actually. Could you please say which sectors these are?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sectors of the Department of Defence were four in number, the security sector; morale and ethics sector; health services sector; and the sector of supply, procurement, and production.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Very briefly, what was the responsibility of the assistant head for security?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assistant head for security was responsible for the administration of the security and information service, as well as for the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Under item VI we see the assistant head for morale had three organisational units under him. We don't need to read them out. It goes on to mention the assistant head for health services who also had three organisational units under him, and then there's the assistant head for supply, procurement, and production, and he had eight organisational units under him. And now under item IX, please explain to us. We saw in item I that the Main Staff is involved in the business of the Department of Defence. Can you please explain item IX of this decision to us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, paragraph IX is, in my opinion, a key paragraph in the text, so please take your time to explain this to us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's remark: Could item IX please be shown on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best, Your Honours. Your Honours, items IX, X, and XI of the part marked B deals with the position of the Main Staff within the Department of Defence. The first sentence says that the Main Staff is undoubtedly part of the Department of Defence. Further on we see that the Main Staff is headed by the Chief of Staff. The Chief of Staff reported to the head of the Department of Defence. He was -- he reported to him about administrative tasks, budget-related issues, material supplies, consumption, and the general organisation of civilian life as well as the wartime organisation of the armed forces. The next paragraph, to my mind, is key to this discussion which has taken quite some time now. Let me read it out, because the sentence speaks for itself: "The chief of Main Staff shall be directly responsible to the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna for all issues relating to the Supreme Command, the organisation or structure of units, strategic and operational plans and the use of the armed forces in time of war or peace. "So the chief of the Main Staff shall exercise superior authority over the command of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, within the scope of general and specific powers vested in him by the President of the HZ HB. "The brigade commanders shall be subordinate and responsible to the president of the HZ HB as a Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I asked you to go slowly because as you said it's crucial, and I agree with you, but please be so kind as to read slowly. The interpreters have just called out for help. You're going too fast. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it follows from this --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I apologise I went quiet because a question was asked by Judge Antonetti, but you did not read out the last part. Could you please read it out so that you can then give us a complete answer.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The brigade commanders shall be subordinate and responsible to the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as the Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces and to the head of the Defence Department and chief of the Main Staff within the scope of their responsibilities, in accordance with the powers described above." From what I've just read, it follows that the Main Staff is a part of the Department of Defence and that the head of the Department of Defence did not have full authority over the Main Staff. The Main Staff is a part of the Department of Defence, but it had a dual position, so to say. So the chief of the Main Staff responds to the head of the Department of Defence when it comes to different professional tasks and administrative tasks. However, as regards the military tasks, he's responsible to the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, who was also the chief of the General Staff. So I believe that the text is clear enough to clarify this certain misunderstanding or doubts that we had earlier. So here we can see how specific was the position of the Main Staff within the Department of Defence, although I believe that at least in some of the countries from which Honourable Judges come the solution may be similar to this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, item X regulates the issue of deputies. Item XI regulates the issues of assistance. And I would just like to show you on -- on the next page, item XIV, which says that the internal organisational structure of the departments and management of the internal structure of the organisational units and other things will be adopted by the head of the department in compliance with the -- I apologise. I tried to read this quickly. Sometimes it seems to me that we lose the sense because we speak too slowly, but, Mr. Marijan, can we just look at the next document, 2D 567. Could you please tell the Honourable Judges what is this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you move on to the next document, I'd like to come back to paragraph IX, which as you pointed out is of paramount importance. You're not lawyer. We all know that, and you said so, but you're an historian. And generally speaking, when you're a specialist in history, you are competent in several fields, among which the military area. According to the text you just read out, the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is the one who has authority over the Main Staff, and it's that head of staff is directly responsible. The word "directly" is actually used. Since this word is used, it means that there is no intermediary between the head of staff and the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. According to you and according to all the documents you've reviewed in the archive, the documents of the Department of Defence, do all these documents illustrate and reflect what is actually stipulated here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can explain this. From my point of view, this is theory or the legal basis, and in practice there are also sufficient number of documents to confirm this. But here I would like to add that the decree on the armed forces, the consolidated version of that decree dated 17 October 1992, in one of its articles stipulated that there was a possibility for the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to delegate some of its authorities concerning the defence and military to the head of the department, but I've never seen that this transfer of responsibility actually took place, because for such powers to be transferred the document should be published in the Official Gazette and there should be information about this sent to all the units. However, this never did happen, so Mr. Stojic was not within the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your conclusion would be as follows: Mr. Stojic did not belong to the head of -- to the chain of command, lines 21, 22, page 14 of the transcript. This is what you say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. You did understand this well. Mr. Stojic was not within the chain of command of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the question that follows would be this one: Mr. Stojic had another function according to you -- sorry, Mr. Prlic was in the chain of command or not. Prlic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic was also not within the chain of command of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to expand one step further. Are you saying -- or what was the situation of the HVO, the "Government of Herceg-Bosna"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The HVO had within its remit the issues related to the defence, so some material provisions, but the way in which the armed forces were to be used was not within their remit. So there is this clear line. The president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, then the chief of the General Staff, and then further on commanders of zones of operations and commanders of brigades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: What does that mean as far as the question of political control of the military is concerned? Normally modern democratic rule of law, doctrine, wants the military to be under control of the political authorities. How did that, if at all, work in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Croatian Community Herceg-Bosna was founded on the basis of a totalitarian and a non-democratic society, so the strategic oversight over the armed forces was meant to be in the hands of the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. However -- or, rather, I'd like to add here something that we mentioned yesterday concerning municipalities. I believe that at the local level there was even too much political influence, and this was damaging as to the effectiveness of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, sorry, I still have some questions on the chain of command. Witness, as far as you know, did the head of the department of the defence have the power to appoint people in top positions in the army? Of course you're not lawyer, but looking at the decree on the armed forces of the community of -- of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Article 34 -- could you please look at Article 34 of this decree on the armed forces and look at the power to appoint people as commanders of the armed forces. Brigade commander, battalion commander, platoon commanders, and so on and so forth. Could you tell us if the head of the department had a say in these appointments?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a point for clarification for the record, which period are we speaking of or which document, Your Honour, because there are two. There's the one back in -- which is P 0289, and then there's P 8 -- P 0588. So which -- which of the two for clarification, because one is in July 1992, and the second one, the P 00588, is later. It's 17 October 1992. So obviously we can see some changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the decree from July the 3rd, 1992, document P 00289.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the first decree which was in force for a relatively short period of time, and in this Article 34, indeed it is stipulated that there is this obligation of the HVO to appoint commanders of brigades, battalions, platoons, and other units. The head of Department of Defence is not mentioned here. He is mentioned, however, in the decree dated the 17th October 1992. So maybe it might be better to have a look at that document if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this article differs from the article contained in the decree dated 3rd of July, 1992, in this part in which it is stipulated that the head of the Department of Defence and the commanders so authorised by him appoint other commanders, officers, non-commissioned officers to different duties. So this is the difference. Here HVO is not mentioned as the executive body but, rather, the head of the Department of Defence. So on the basis of this article and on the basis of what happened in practice, I can say that the head of the Department of Defence did not appoint high-ranking commanders, for example, commanders of zones of operations and commanders of brigades. Later in the report I mentioned an example that the head of the Department of Defence was authorised to appoint all officers but one, and that one was the brigade commander. This was the responsibility of the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give us an example? Petar Kresimir Brigade commander, you were a soldier in that brigade. As far as you know, was this commander directly appointed by Mr. Boban, and could you tell us the name of your -- the name of the commander of the Kresimir Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the first commander of the Petar Kresimir, the 4th Brigade, and he was the commander during the period more or less to which I refer in my report, was Stanko Vrgoc. He was a company commander, reserve company commander on the Territorial Defence -- or, sorry, reserve company captain in the Territorial Defence. I would not say the truth if I was to say that I saw any document appointing him to that position, but I have no doubt that he was indeed appointed by Mr. Boban. From that period and the period immediately thereafter, we have sufficient proof to be able to make such a claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, the text of Article 34(2) of the decree of October 1992 is very clear. One does not have to be a lawyer to read that commanders of brigades shall be appointed or replaced by the head of the Defence Department. You tell us that the reality was a different one, so as an observer one starts to wonder what's the worth of these so-called legal texts if they are not respected. What -- is there any rule? Can you explain this? How come? Are any rules respected? How can one know whether a rule is in fact a rule or just something written on paper?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me, I believe this might be helpful. We talked about this on several occasions already, and we pointed out that there was a problem in translation. So the text that you are actually reading is not fully corresponding to the text of the decree. So if you allow me, I would like to go back to the text of the decree dated 3rd July, but please just bear in mind that in October the responsibilities that were previously held by HVO were now held by the head of the Department of Defence. And if you look at that text, at the text of the decree dated 3rd of July, it will be much clearer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, Your Honours, I would kindly ask you here concerning this text, and we also already proposed another document because next week we will have another witness, the witness who actually drafted this decree before it was adopted, and we offered to the Judges Article 34 with correct interpunction, correct punctuation, because there is a problem with punctuation in this translation. So if you were to read this translation, but even in Croatian, it would result that the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was not appointing anybody, but if you allow Mr. Marijan to explain what the real meaning of this article was, he will explain the meaning of Article 34 regardless of the punctuation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you just read in your own language Article 34, because I had my colleague's question, and now I have a doubt. So could you please read out in your own language Article 34 as it is currently on your screen. Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 34 reads as follows: "The commanders in the armed forces shall be appointed and dismissed by the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Commanders of brigades and officers at higher positions by the head of the Department of Defence or commanders so authorised by him. Other officers and commanders, non-commissioned officers, military servants to --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Marijan, but I believe in the English translation it doesn't -- didn't come through that -- in the second point of Article 34. You had not -- either you have not mentioned or the translation did not, in a way, contain that commanders, and I quote now: "Commanders of brigades and high-ranking officers shall be appointed or replaced by the head of the Defence Department." It was not mentioned in the English translation before. "Or by commanders appointed by him." So it is only a translation problem which I would have liked to point out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please read out slowly the second bullet point, because we have an edge there because there is a translation directly into English but also directly into French, which enables us to understand better. So please read out that second paragraph which may be of paramount importance. Read it out slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my feeling is that the interpreters are reading the texts from the decree rather than the texts as spoken by our witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking the interpreters not to look at the English text, please. The witness is actually reading. This is the reason why I asked the witness to read slowly, so that we have the direct interpretation of --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe this could be helpful: I believe that the key issue is that the interpreters and -- are putting the punctuation or ending the sentences on their own without the witness putting a full stop or finishing a sentence. So I would kindly ask the witness to put the punctuation marks where he believes they should stand, so colon, semicolon, or comma or the full stop so that we know which sentence ends where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I do not understand why the witness should put in the punctuation where he thinks it should be. Either it is here or it is not. If it is not here, then he should not simulate it. But to let the witness put in commas and dots in a text, I think that would not be quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm merely saying that the witness is reading -- or should -- should read the punctuation rather than leaving it to the interpreters and the court reporter to put punctuation as they think fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please read out the text as we see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it might be best since this is about appointing and relieving of duty. When I mention, say, president of the HZ HB appoints and relieves of duty and continue reading this -- I believe then it would be clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you start reading Article 34 over again slowly, please. What I'm asking you is not complicated. I just want you to read the text, please. If I spoke your language, I could read it out myself, but I'm sure everyone would snicker. That's why I prefer that you read the text. Otherwise, I can ask Madam Nozica to read. A six-year-old child could read and do what I'm asking. Just read the text as it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Commanders in the armed forces shall be appointed and relieved of their duties as follows: "The president of the HZ HB," here there should be a comma, "appoints and relieves of their duty brigade commanders and higher-ranking officers. "The head of the Department of Defence and the commanders authorised by him shall appoint and relieve of their duty other officers and commanders, non-commissioned officers, military servants to officers -- officers' positions and positions of non-commissioned officers." This is what it should be -- should read, and there is enough evidence for that in practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The organisation of this article, which could be a French article, for that matter, distinguishes clearly between the president of the HVO, the -- or, rather, the president who appoints the commanders and high-ranking officers and the head of the department, in this case Mr. Stojic when he was appointed to this position. Who appoints the other officers and non-commissioned officers, et cetera? The result is that it is Mr. Boban who appoints the commanders of the brigades and the high-ranking officers and that the head of the department appoints the other officers. That is what this Article 34 states, and that's why in your own language there is a reference to appointment and revocation and then a list of the various positions and the individuals who come under the responsibility. So me for me this article is quite clear. Maybe it's not clear for everyone in the courtroom, but it's up to each and every one of us to reflect upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A number of pages ago, and at least a dozen speakers intervening in between, I asked a question; and all that has happened in between does not give me the impression that the question was besides the point. It still appears to me that the decree clearly says that it is the head of the Defence Department who nominates chiefs of brigades and other superior officers. To some extent he can delegate this. I'm a bit astonished that you changed the interpunction of the law as if you could make it suit own thesis. I remain with the impression that this law was not respected in practice, and I wonder what your explanation is for this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters remark: The witness was reading a different text from that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the problem is exactly with the punctuation. This Official Gazette not in the least is full of such problems. You can find them in various places. And just like the Defence counsel said, the question here is who is appointed by the HZ HB at all if we rely on the punctuation as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd just like to mention that there was a comment by the interpreter which is quite crucial who says that the witness was reading a different text from what was on the screen. So I wonder now which text he actually read out, which exhibit he has been reading out.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to mention on the record that counsel is correct. Witness was reading from Article 34 of P -- P 289 instead of 588. Sorry, it's the other way around actually. Article 34 of P 588 instead of P 289. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But that was in fact the one he was supposed to read.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow, we had this kind of situation also when we were examining Mr. Tomljanovich, and it was because of wrong punctuation and badly typed text. So I ask you now for permission to continue, because the witness was saying what it really should be like. He was not reading Article 34, and he actually added a final comment, "This is how it should be," because the punctuation in Article 34 of the decree under Exhibit P 00588 is wrong. I ask you to accept what the witness says as correct, because he thinks that that is what it should read. This is what it should be like. If we were to read Article 34 of the decree dated October the way it is printed with the period there, that would strictly speaking mean that the president of the HZ HB doesn't appoint anybody at all. That's the problem with the punctuation. Next week the witness who worked in drafting this text will be here. I don't like to do this, but anyway, there was a typing error in the drafting of this text. It is very logical, and for logical reasons the witness does not refuse to read the text as it is, but he -- he really says that this is what the text should be like, and for the Defence there is no doubt whatsoever that that is indeed the case. We can make another comparison and read the text literally, and if you allow, I will do that, the text from the decree dated the 3rd of July, Exhibit P 289 where the punctuation is correct. Only in that decree, instead of the head of the department what is stated there is the HVO. So we can do that or alternatively accept the witness's statement which is a logical interpretation of the decree as it was written when it comes to language, from the point of view of language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, I propose that we simply go on now. I do not think -- we would -- we would have to go pretty far. The witness says without some -- any further foundation that the text should be something different than what we see, and you promised that the next witness will explain that. So I think we lose time if I insist, and I would suggest that we leave it at that and go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. We shall leave it at this point, but for the minutes, for the summary record, Article 34 is included in a document that we all have, which is the text which was published in the official journals, the Official Gazette. Article 34 is on page 0026-7318. And when I examine Article 34, and there's no doubt about its content because this is the text that was published, I can see clearly that it's not identical to the one that was on the screen a few moments ago, because on the screen there were three indents, an additional one, whereas in the official text there are only two subparagraphs, two indents. So perhaps the Registrar could display page 0026-7318 in B/C/S. Everyone could see that clearly, and we would indeed be able to save time. So here it is. We can see the article. There's no doubt here that it's different. And you see there are not three indents but only two. So, Witness -- Witness, could you please read out this official version of Article 34, because was this -- was this the text that you read a moment ago? In that case, could you confirm that the text you read out a few moments ago was indeed this text and not the other text that we had on the e-court screen? Fine. Madam Nozica, we have the official Article 34, and that is the one that the witness read out a few moments ago. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, only I'm not sure what you expect now. Should I read the text, or what do you expect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue. Do as you like. You're using your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that a large part of this discussion should not count against my time, because I wouldn't have allowed to -- to spend so much time on this, because things are very clear here and will become more clear once we hear subsequent witnesses. Let us now see what this expert witness will tell us, and the Chamber will decide whose evidence to trust.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, you said to us that in Article 34, irrespective of the punctuation errors, the intention was to stipulate that the commanders of the armed forces shall be organised and relieved of duty by the president of the HZ HB, whereas brigade commanders and high-ranking officers shall be appointed or replaced by the head of the Department of Defence. Now, I will show you some other documents, but tell us now whether you agree with my statement as put now. Mr. Marijan, you keep looking at the transcript all the time, wait for everything to appear on the screen, and then you make pauses and that's why the Honourable Judge Antonetti got the impression that you were trying to make up your mind whether to -- whether or not to say something. Do not bother with the transcript. Just make sure to allow some time to elapse after my question and before you answer. If anything is wrong with the transcript, we will intervene. You just limit yourself to answering questions with a delay of about 30 seconds, say.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my conclusion is that the president of HZ HB under this article appointed and relieved of duty brigade commanders and officers in high-ranking positions and which can be easily shown, and practice was like that indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So the documents shown fully corroborate your interpretation of Article 34. Isn't it -- isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Your interpretation of Article 34 is that the head of the Department of Defence or persons authorised by him were able to appoint other officers and commanders, non-commissioned officers and military servants to officers' duties and duties of non-commissioned officers in the armed forces. So did the head of the Department of Defence indeed appoint and relieve these persons that I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the documents that I saw are fully in line with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us get back to the structure of the Department of Defence, which brought us to this topic. So let me go back. The decision about the structure of the Department of Defence passed by President Boban in September, on the 15th of September, 1992, and by this decision he ordered the head of the Department of Defence to implement this internal structure. This decision is 2D 567. Could you give us a short comment of item I of this decision, because it contains some important points for subsequent personnel policy. We see who the head appoints and what the internal structure of the department is like.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the decision of Mr. Stojic, dated October 17th, 1992, regulates the internal structure of the department, that is the internal organisation of sectors, administrations, officers, and the Main Staff of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please be as precise as possible.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item III reads: "A special structure is in place for the Main Staff, and that structure is part of this Decision." I must add that I have not seen this part.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So item I says that the assistant heads are responsible for the functioning of the individual sectors in line with the guide-lines set by the head of the Department of Defence and the adopted work plan.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now there's a segment. Please explain to us what this is about. The administration for defence-related issues and mobilisation. Then budget, the staff of civil protection, the administration for legal affairs, personnel affairs. Persons in charge of this are the heads of these respective units and report to the head of the department.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters would apologise, but we did not get the answer or the last part of the question. Could it be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please tell us briefly about the Main Staff, what this is and how certain persons are selected to work in the Main Staff. Perhaps this will clarify somewhat the provisions of Article 34 of the decree on the armed forces which is -- still seems unclear to some. So please explain to us the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we have just said, there was a special structure if place for the Main Staff which is an integral part of this decision. It should have been enclosed, but as I've said, I haven't seen it. The part relating to the Main Staff here deals with the appointment of persons to the Main Staff, who is in charge of that, and from that we can understand the structure of the Main Staff of the HVO as it was then. So there is a statement that the chief of Main Staff has a deputy who is appointed by the president of the HZ HB upon the proposal of the Chief of Main Staff or with the approval of the head of the Defence Department. In the following paragraphs the units of the Main Staff are mentioned, the operational section, operational centre, the Military Intelligence Service, the assistant heads of -- for reserve, assistant or Home Guard assistant chief for organisation, personnel and legal affairs, assistant chief for special purpose units, they're all appointed by the president of the HZ HB upon the proposal of the chief of the Main Staff and with the approval of the head of the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, all these persons and positions that you mentioned, are these higher-ranking officers as -- in accordance with the language of Article 34 of the decree on the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are heads of the departments of the Main Staff and assistant heads. So I'm speaking about the Main Staff as an umbrella organisation of the armed forces. So this cannot be interpreted in any other way than -- than as referring to high-ranking officers. This can also be verified. I believe that the formation of the Main Staff is contained in the documents also, and they are -- all these officers are majors, lieutenant-colonels and colonels.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: About all the other appointments, other heads and assistant heads in the Main Staff are appointed by who?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other heads and assistant heads in the Main Staff are appointed by the head of the Department of Defence upon the proposal of the Chief of Staff. Let me say this is a possibility. At the moment when this decision was adopted, the Main Staff didn't have any more departments or sections than these. And in the final part of this paragraph, it says that other operatives and employees of the Main Staff are assigned by the Chief of the -- of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we now briefly describe the situation in the security sector?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Appointments in the security sector in principle are made upon the proposal of the assistant head of the Department of Defence for security. This goes for higher-ranking officers. And lower-ranking officers are appointed by the assistant head but with the approval of the head of the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us be precise. It says assistant heads of sector for analysis and -- analysis-related business and assistant heads for operational -- for operations, et cetera, are appointed by the head of the department and lower-ranking officers by the assistant himself but with the approval of the head.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but about lower-ranking officers we must stress that the head must approve their appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Nozica, you have an hour and 30 minutes remaining. We are going to try to keep to the timing. Of course the Judges can also always make comments, but I will try to discipline myself and let you continue, because indeed sometimes we may have many questions on a particular text, but we cannot necessarily ask all of the questions that come to mind for reasons of time. We shall now have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, we have a rather difficult task ahead of us. The time is short, and we have to go through most of your report, so we'll try to do this together. In this document, and we are talking about the document 2D 00567, this is the Decision on the Internal Structure of the Department of Defence, dated 17th October, 1992, that was cosigned by Mr. Mate Boban on 10th of November, 1992. We've come to the security sector. You explained who appointed officials to this security sector. In order to make this clear, when it comes to the assistant heads for security in the staff of the zones of operation, it says here that they're appointed by the deputy following a recommendation of the head; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The same goes for assistants for security at the brigade levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Furthermore, here we see how the appointments are made for heads of sectors of general affairs, and now we can move to the health service sector. When it comes to the health service sector, can you simply give us the principle?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the heads of services within the health sector were appointed by the head of the Department of Defence following a proposal made by the assistant head for health services. Other officials or lower-ranking officials within the sector were appointed by the assistant head for health services with the approval of the head of Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to the sector for morale, can you give us a brief explanation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the situation was more or less similar, and the situation was more or less similar in the sector for procurement and production. So the appointments were made by the head of department following the proposal made by the assistant head for that particular sector, and lower-ranking officials were appointed by the assistant head for a particular sector with the approval of the head of department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When it comes to item VI, we are still talking about the sector for morale. The assistant commander for morale for the zone of operations and furthermore as it stands here in the document, could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So within the units of the armed forces of the HZ HB there were assistant commanders for morale, and they were appointed by the head of the Department for Defence following the proposal made by the assistant head of department for morale.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained what it was like in the logistics, procurement, and production sector.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what the administrations and offices for defence were.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The heads of administrations for defence at the time when this decision was made, there were four such administrations, and they were appointed by the HVO. So this -- these were the only positions to which people were appointed by the HVO as stipulated by this decision following a proposal made by the head of the Department of Defence. The heads of offices for defence, which were a lower organisational unit, they were appointed by the head of the Department of Defence following a proposal made by the relevant -- by the head of the relevant administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: With this we've rounded up the issues regulated by this decision. This decision also regulates what is done by each of these sectors, what are their tasks, and you've analysed this in your report. Did you also use this decision as a source for your report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The remit of different organisational units of the Department of Defence is stipulated in the decision made by Mr. Boban on the 15th of November, and it also results from the decree on the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In order to have a complete picture, can we also mention another decision, Decision on the Internal Organisation of the Department of Defence, dated 20th of May, 1993. This is the next decision in your binder. Can you just point out the differences between these two decisions in order not to spend too much time on this issue?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In line 34, 8, it says 15th November, and this should be corrected. The decision dated the 20th of May, 1993, differs from the previous one in the following: It is much more logical in its wording. Most provisions -- or most of the provisions are the same, but now we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can I just ask which exhibit number we're referring to, please. We're talking about a decision, but we don't have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you're talking about decisions, please could you give us the exhibit number and make sure it is in the transcript, because sometimes it doesn't appear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said it, and I think the witness understood it. This is P 02477. That is the exhibit number. I'm sorry, I did not want to interrupt the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You may continue now.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this decision dated the 20th of May, the novelty is the welfare administration which comes under the authority of the civilian sector. And another novelty is the central logistics base in the sector for logistics procurement and production. These are the only two novelties.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, in your report, starting in item 18, you explain what were the tasks of the civilian sector. I will have to be very quick, so I would just like to point out the items that my questions will refer to. In item 20, you are talking about the chief of administration for compulsory military service and administration. I asked you when this administration became operational, and you said that here. Could you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The administration for compulsory military service and administration started to function in July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. In your report, in item 21, you say that a personnel administration was established on the 8th of May, 1992, two months before the establishment of the Department of Defence. This is document 2D 1458. You will also see it on your screen. Because the time is very short, can you please just confirm that this was the source for this conclusion you made here?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the source for my conclusion. I remember this document, although I cannot see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You will be able to see it very soon.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of the first administrations that were established by the HVO, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We shall now say a few words about administrations and offices for defence. Can you tell us very quickly what were offices -- what were administrations for defence, and what were their main tasks? Just the main tasks, please, because they will be most relevant for our discussion.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Defence administrations carried out professional tasks within the Department of Defence. So here you have a list of tasks, but the most relevant were the maintenance of manning levels, mobilisation of the armed forces. So this was the main task to take care about personnel issues and material procurement within the territory under their competence. There were four such administrations that covered the territory of a zone of operations, and the lower level in their organisational structure was the defence office.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We shall now move on to the security sector. This is item 30 of your report. Can you just tell us what the security sector was composed of? What were its components?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security sector was composed of the Security and Information Service and the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me who appointed Mr. Coric, just to make it very brief? And this is document 2D 1333. I'm now moving quickly and skipping some of the documents, but this is two documents later, and we will be able to see that on the e-court. So could you please tell me who appointed the assistant head for security.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the first appointments ever made by -- in the HVO that I saw, made on 13th of April, 1992. Mr. Boban, who was the head of the HVO at the time, appointed Mr. Coric to the position of assistant commander for Security and Information Service, and he was also in charge of all the units of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When was the assistant for security appointed?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assistant for security was appointed by the HVO in October of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In item 32 you explained the structure of the security sector. Since we already saw who was making the appointments, when it comes to the security sector could you precisely state that the assistant commanders in the zones of operations -- or, actually, we'll leave it for now. Can you just tell me very quickly what was the main structure of the security sector?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security sector consisted of the administration for security and information and the military police administration. I already stated that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. You said in your report, in item 32, that there were attempts to subordinate the military police to the commander in charge of the Security and Information Service. Then in item 34 and 35 of your report, you explained how come that these particular organisational structure within -- within the department was established and how different it was from the previous system, but could you please briefly explain what were the tasks of the Security and Information Service and of the military police. So could you tell us which particular provision of the decree on the armed forces stipulates these tasks? And I'm referring here to item 36 of your -- or 37 of your report.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Article 137 of the decree on the armed forces from October 1992 regulates this. It states that professional work related to security of the armed forces and the Defence Department shall be organised and performed by the Security and Information Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would just like to mention that this is the document P 588, so that we can all follow the wording of the decree. So this is Article 137 of the document P 588. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same article it is stated that the armed forces shall include military police who will be in charge of security in military traffic, of military order and discipline, and elimination of criminal elements in the armed forces. So my conclusion would be that the military police was treated as an integral part of the armed forces, whereas the Security and Information Service was active both within the armed forces and within the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now we shall move to the part of your report entitled, "The Security and Information Service." I would just like to ask something in relation to item 39 of your report. Could you tell me very briefly what the SIS consisted of.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Security and Information System consisted of its administration, SIS centres, and SIS officers at the commands of armed forces units.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the chain of command, who were these SIS officers at the commands of units subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SIS officers at the level of units were subordinated to the commander of the respective unit, and at the professional level they responded to their superior within the Security and Information Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In your report you stated that within the units the higher position they could have was at the command level, at the level of the command of the zones of operation. In the documents that you worked on, could you see that there was an assistant for the Security and Information Service also at the level of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- in the documents I could see that there was such an assistant in the -- in the year 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to this because there is no document proving this fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if we look at the document 2D 944, although I believe this is a question for cross-examination, that's why I didn't want to spend too much time on this, but if we could take a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document that stands outside the time-frame that is testified about by this witness. The witness stated that he is witnessing about the events until about 15th of November, and this is the document dated 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... time-frame. It is a matter of principle, so let's see what the witness has to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. However, I believe that this document refers to the previous period, to the situation during the previous period, so I believe we should allow the witness to testify about this, and later on we shall also have other witnesses testifying about this, including Mr. Ivan Bandic, who is mentioned here. So possibly we can see what this witness based his conclusion on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yet another objection. The question refers to the assistant head -- or Chief of the Main Staff, and in this document Chief of the Main Staff -- or assistant Chief of the Main Staff isn't mentioned. So I believe we should be very precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, you heard all these objections. So you are talking here about assistant for SIS, Security and Information Service. Bearing in mind all the previous objections, could you please tell us what this statement of yours is based upon?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this statement is based upon these documents. This document was created four days after Mr. Stojic ceased to be head of the Department of Defence, but towards the end of this document we can see that most of the people mentioned at the time were holding their positions for quite some time so it provides a picture of the previous period. Also if somebody is the top official of the Security and Information Service at the Main Staff level, then I cannot come to a different conclusion than that he was an assistant for the SIS, but I really cannot give you a clear formation of the Main Staff because I've never seen the formation of the Main Staff at the time, whether this was called a department or something else I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that he was an assistant for the SIS. From what you just said I can conclude that you have no doubts that such a position existed even earlier in the second half of 1993. You just have doubts as to the title of this position, whether this was an assistant or something else.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, my only doubt is the status so -- the position, but the fact is that that person was at the level of the Main Staff and some administrative clerks are also mentioned here. Generally speaking, I am aware of the structure of different departments or sections, as they were called, but to be truthful, the Main Staff at that time included also two duties which were not officially in the formation. Neither the chief or the deputy chief were ever mentioned in any formation. However, somebody appointed them and other people did accept them as such, with such titles.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We can now move on to the part of your report talking about the military police, item 43 and onwards. I can see here that you've provided us with the entire structure of the military police. You've mentioned all the different parts of the military police, including the active part, brigade level, military police, and I do not want to spend too much time here. I would just like your confirmation that this part of your report is also based on the documents that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my entire report is based on the documents. I don't believe that I used any secondary source.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When it comes to the sector for morale that is referred to in item 53 of your report, could you tell us how was this sector organised and who the assistants for morale at the level of the units were subordinated to.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sector for morale was in charge of boosting morale and promotion of information and preparation for defence. It consisted of three administrations, and there were also assistants of commanders for morale at the level of different units. So this was very similar to the security service. The head of the sector for morale was appointed by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the influence of these assistants for morale or assistants for information and propaganda service?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that on the basis of the documents you could really assess their impact. On the basis of my personal experience I believe that the impact was not very great. The information service was rather poor, and there was an administration for military psychology, for example, which at war times is not particularly a pertinent topic, and in the entire territory of HVO there were only two psychologists. I know them personally. There wasn't much use of them. So generally speaking, I believe that their influence was rather poor. And not much changed in the period when I was there in 1994 and 1995 in the department which was later called Department for Political Management. The only requirement was that people working there had -- had a university diploma and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Because you were there, could you tell us when it comes to the activities of this sector could you say that they promoted the hate speech or any other inappropriate language in their programmes, in their -- in their addresses to the people or anything that they were doing?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said already that at the time when I was in Livno, I had a feeling that this service did not exist at all. The only thing that I knew about this was that my school colleague actually worked for that service. That's how I knew that it did exist. I cannot say that there were no individuals who possibly used the hate speech, but this was certainly not the predominant tone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. We will move on to the health service sector which you explain entirely. In reference to the item 67 of your report, can you tell us that health services existed within the armed force and in which way were they organised?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A unit at the level of brigade, for example, had a head of medical staff, and he was part of the logistics at the brigade level.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I will move on to the sector for supply, procurement, and production that you deal with starting in item 73 of your report. I would like to ask a few questions in reference to item 77 of your report where you quote the annual report of the Defence Department. This is document P 8118. My question will be based on your report. These are parts of the mentioned report in English. These are pages 7 to 10 which talk about the structure of expenses and the structure of revenues. Here you stated that it follows from this annual report that the revenue that came from the Republic of Croatia amounted to approximately 10 per cent of the total amount. On the basis your personal experience, could you tell us in which way did the funds come to the banks of the Croatian State which were also intended for the defence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? On the basis of your personal experience, and could you try to be as concise as possible.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I come from the area of Livno, and Livno is an area in which majority of the population live outside of the territory of the municipality than within the municipality. Many of these people worked, and they still do, in Germany. This was a trend present ever since 1960s. Livno was not an exclusive example. This was a general occurrence, not only in Bosnia-Herzegovina but also in Croatia. I'm very familiar with the security and political and military situation in the Republic of Croatia between 1991 and 1995. So during the war, Croatia was broken into different parts. The tourism, which was the main source of revenue, was totally destroyed, and the only financial source which allowed Croatia to sustain itself through the war was the money that came from abroad. Not only from people who were working abroad, but also from -- from the Croatian diaspora. So second or third generation Croats who live abroad. Obviously this money was intended for the defence of Croatia and the Croats. So I believe that these 10 per cent came, although I believe that the percentage of people sending money who originated from Bosnia and Herzegovina was actually much higher than 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If I understood well, you are saying that Croats who lived in Bosnia and Herzegovina and who were sending the money sent much more than the amount quoted here as the amount that was given by Croatia for the purpose of the defence.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no doubt about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, do you know if these people, the emigrants who worked abroad, that they sent money purposely for the HVO or the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak about everybody, but I do know that in a part of the municipality there was this financial obligation. You could talk about war taxation. So able-bodied people who could be able to fight but were not there but were working in Germany at the time, they were obliged to send a certain amount of money to the account of the HVO Livno, and this was the money that was used for the defence of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I do not have enough time to ask about any details concerning the accounts, numbers of accounts, and so on, so we will move on to the Main Staff of the HVO. This is the item 83 of your report, but thanks to the previous questions by Honourable Judges we've clarified most of it already. In item 86 of your report, could you please tell us what was your conclusion in this item.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In item 86 I comment on the relationship between the head of the Department of Defence and the Chief of the Main Staff according to the provisions of the decree that we saw. There's no doubt that the Chief of Main Staff reported to the head of the Department of Defence with regard to the supply of materiel, that is, the supply of weapons, ammunition, fuel, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You mentioned in this item that the Chief of Staff was responsible to the head of the Department of Defence for all administrative work as well as issues concerning the budgetary and the materiel supply and consumption.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you refer to the decision on the basic principles of the organisation of the Department of Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us now look at document P 4131. That's the first document in binder two. We skipped all the documents in between and will not return to them. Do you have these documents in front of you? These are the documents that you dealt with, so you can consult them directly. Have you found them?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you comment? Is this the line of command that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the line of command at the beginning of the first half -- yes, you could say that this is the line of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You were saying from the second half. What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the line of command from the second half of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
